body:
Eastern India: rice, rivers and regional customs

Bengal

Bengal's riverine plains and deltaic environment support rice cultivation and fishing. Consequently, rice and fish have historically occupied an important place in Bengali food traditions.

Fish preparation appears in Bengali literature and historical terracotta artwork. A terracotta plaque at the Vishalakshi temple in Arambagh depicts fish being prepared for household consumption.

Bengal is also associated with milk-based sweets, including sandesh and rasogolla, and with rice preparations such as panta bhaat, in which cooked rice is soaked and allowed to ferment.

The Brihaddharma Purana

The Brihaddharma Purana, a Sanskrit text composed in Bengal in the 13th century, permitted local Brahmanas to consume certain varieties of fish. This historical example illustrates how established regional food practices could influence religious dietary conventions.

The permission was specific to certain fish and a particular regional context. It should not be interpreted as a general rule concerning the diet of Brahmanas throughout India.

Odisha

Rice is an important staple in Odisha. Pakhala is a preparation of cooked rice served with water, often after fermentation. Odisha also has important temple-food traditions and a variety of rice-based cakes known as pitha.

At the Jagannath Temple in Puri, the food offered to the deity and subsequently distributed to devotees is known as Mahaprasad. This illustrates the connection between food, pilgrimage and religious community life.

Bihar

Bihar is associated with litti chokha. Litti consists of dough balls commonly stuffed with seasoned sattu, while chokha is a mashed vegetable preparation, often made from roasted brinjal, potatoes or tomatoes.

Sattu is flour prepared from roasted ingredients, commonly roasted gram. It is distinct from ordinary besan, which is generally prepared by grinding unroasted gram.

Southern India: rice, millets and coastal resources

Rice is widely used in southern Indian cuisines, although millets also have important regional roles. Coconut, tamarind, curry leaves, pulses and various spices contribute to distinctive culinary traditions.

Tamil Nadu

Idli, dosa and sambar are important examples. Traditional idli and dosa are commonly prepared from fermented rice-and-urad-dal batter. Idli is steamed, whereas dosa is cooked on a heated griddle. Sambar is a lentil-based preparation containing vegetables and seasonings, commonly including tamarind.

Pongal is both the name of a harvest festival and the name of rice-based preparations associated with Tamil Nadu. Sweet pongal commonly contains rice, pulses and jaggery.

Karnataka

Finger millet, known as ragi, is traditionally important in parts of Karnataka. Ragi mudde consists of cooked finger millet flour formed into balls.

Bisi bele bath is a rice-and-lentil preparation commonly cooked with vegetables and spices. Mysore pak is a sweet associated with Mysuru, traditionally prepared using gram flour, sugar and ghee.

Kerala

Kerala's coastal environment and coconut cultivation influence its food traditions. Appam is a rice-based pancake, while puttu is a steamed preparation of rice flour, commonly layered with coconut.

Sadya is a traditional vegetarian feast commonly served on a banana leaf. It is especially associated with Onam and ceremonial occasions. Its vegetarian character does not imply that all Kerala cuisine is vegetarian; fish and meat preparations are also important in several communities.

Andhra Pradesh and Telangana

Rice, pulses, chillies and sour ingredients are important in many local food traditions. Andhra cuisine is known for preparations using gongura, a sour leafy vegetable.

Hyderabadi biryani is closely associated with Hyderabad in Telangana and reflects the city's historical courtly culinary traditions.

Northeastern India

Northeastern India contains numerous ethnic communities and distinct ecological zones. Rice is important across much of the region, while bamboo shoots, local vegetables, fish, fermented foods and smoked foods feature in different community traditions.

In Assam, rice cakes known as pitha are associated with Bihu festivities. In Mizoram, bai is a preparation commonly containing vegetables, bamboo shoots and local herbs; some versions also contain meat. Sikkim and other Himalayan areas have traditions of fermenting vegetables and soybean products.

Fermented and preserved foods illustrate the use of inherited knowledge to make seasonal resources available in different periods and to create distinctive flavours.

Prelims focus

  • The 13th-century Brihaddharma Purana permitted certain fish for Bengal Brahmanas.
  • Litti chokha is associated with Bihar and commonly uses sattu.
  • Pakhala is a rice preparation associated with Odisha.
  • Idli is steamed, while dosa is cooked on a griddle.
  • Sadya is a traditional vegetarian feast associated with Kerala.
  • Pongal is associated with Tamil Nadu, while pitha is important in Assamese Bihu celebrations.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts – II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 9, Fish as Food, p. 135; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 8, pp. 127–128 and 131–132; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Food sections for the relevant states; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, East and South regional culinary profiles; Kerala Tourism, traditional cuisine and festival-food sections. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Distinctive characteristics of Gujarati food

Gujarati cuisine is known for its extensive vegetarian traditions, varied preparations of cereals and pulses, dairy products, vegetables and savoury snacks. Many dishes combine sweet, sour, salty and spicy flavours.

Vegetarian traditions have been influenced by agricultural conditions and religious practices, including Jain and Vaishnava dietary customs. Nevertheless, Gujarat also has important non-vegetarian food traditions among several coastal, tribal, Muslim and other communities.

Gujarati cuisine is widely associated with vegetarian food, but vegetarianism is neither universal across Gujarat nor sufficient to describe the state's entire culinary heritage.

Structure of the Gujarati thali

A thali is a complete meal served on a platter, commonly containing several dishes and accompaniments. The Gujarati thali combines staple grains, pulses, vegetables, dairy preparations, snacks and sweets.

  • Rotli or rotlo: Flatbreads made from wheat or millets.
  • Bhaat or khichdi: Cooked rice or a combined rice-and-pulse preparation.
  • Dal: A cooked pulse preparation, frequently made from tur dal.
  • Kadhi: A preparation commonly made from curd or buttermilk and gram flour.
  • Shaak: A cooked vegetable preparation.
  • Kathol: Whole-pulse preparations using beans, chickpeas or other legumes.
  • Farsan: Savoury snacks that may be steamed, fried or otherwise cooked.
  • Mishthaan: Sweet preparations such as shrikhand, basundi or lapsi.
  • Accompaniments: Pickles, chutneys, salad, papad and chaas.

The exact combination depends on the region, season, household and occasion. Sweets may be served as part of the meal rather than exclusively after the main course.

Traditional Gujarati breads

BreadPrincipal ingredient or feature
RotliThin, unleavened wheat flatbread
Bajri no rotloThick pearl millet flatbread
Juwar no rotloSorghum flatbread
Nagli no rotloFinger millet flatbread
BhakhriGenerally thicker and firmer flatbread
TheplaSeasoned flatbread, often made with fenugreek leaves
KhakhraThin, dry and crisp roasted flatbread

Thepla, khakhra and certain varieties of dhebra are convenient travel foods. Their relative portability and keeping qualities make them useful during journeys and pilgrimage.

Farsan and other savoury preparations

PreparationIdentifying characteristic
DhoklaSteamed cake traditionally made from fermented grain-and-pulse batter
KhamanSoft steamed preparation made primarily from gram
KhandviThin, soft rolls commonly made from gram flour and curd
PatraColocasia leaves layered with seasoned gram-flour batter, rolled and cooked
FafdaLong, crisp, fried gram-flour snack
GanthiyaFried gram-flour snack
HandvoSavoury grain-and-pulse cake, often containing vegetables
KhichuSoft, seasoned dough preparation, commonly made with rice flour

Traditional dhokla commonly combines grains such as rice with pulses, whereas khaman is characteristically gram-based. Modern recipes and local naming conventions may overlap, but the 2 preparations are not identical.

Traditional sweets

Gujarati sweet preparations make extensive use of milk, curd, ghee, flour, sugar and jaggery. Shrikhand is made from strained curd, basundi from thickened milk, and lapsi commonly from broken wheat. Mohanthal is a gram-flour-based sweet.

Prelims focus

  • Rotlo is commonly made from millets, while rotli is generally wheat-based.
  • Kadhi is primarily a curd or buttermilk and gram-flour preparation.
  • Kathol refers to pulse preparations, whereas shaak refers to vegetables.
  • Patra is characteristically prepared with colocasia leaves.
  • Khakhra is a dry, crisp flatbread suitable for travel.
  • Trap: Khaman and traditional dhokla are related but distinct preparations.

[References: Gujarat Tourism, Gujarati Cuisines, Gujarati Thali, Khaman, Khandvi, Patra, Fafda, Rotlo and festival and seasonal fare sections; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Gujarati-Food; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Food section; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Food Trail: Eat Your Way Through Surat's Gastronomic Delights. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Gujarati Cuisine: The Thali, Breads and Traditional Snacks

body:
Regional variations within Gujarat

Gujarat contains dry grasslands, fertile agricultural plains, coastal areas and forested hills. These different environments have contributed to distinctive local cuisines. Historical trade, migration and neighbouring cultures have further enriched regional food traditions.

Saurashtra or Kathiawad

The relatively dry environment of Saurashtra favours traditional reliance on crops such as bajra. Kathiawadi cuisine is particularly associated with bajri no rotlo, pulses, buttermilk and strongly flavoured vegetable preparations.

Popular combinations include rotlo with ringan no olo, a roasted and mashed brinjal preparation, and garlic chutney. Sev tameta nu shaak combines tomatoes with sev, which consists of thin fried gram-flour noodles.

Garlic, red chillies and other spices contribute to the characteristic strong flavours of many Kathiawadi dishes.

Kutch

The arid and semi-arid environment of Kutch has supported millet-based food traditions, dairy products and the use of ingredients with suitable keeping qualities. Rotlo, khichdi, kadhi and buttermilk are familiar elements of traditional Kutchi meals.

Dabeli is a popular snack associated with Kutch. It consists of a spiced potato filling served inside a bread bun, commonly accompanied by chutneys, roasted peanuts and pomegranate seeds.

North and Central Gujarat

North Gujarat has important traditions of millet flatbreads and dairy products, reflecting agricultural and livestock-based livelihoods. Wheat, bajra, pulses and vegetables are widely used across North and Central Gujarat.

The Gujarati thali, with its combination of dal, kadhi, shaak, rotli, rice and farsan, is especially useful for understanding the shared culinary traditions of these regions. Its precise composition varies between communities.

South Gujarat and Surat

South Gujarat has a relatively wetter climate than the northwestern parts of the state. Rice, jowar, vegetables and seasonal agricultural produce contribute to its culinary diversity. Its proximity to Maharashtra also influences some regional food practices.

Surat is an important centre of food traditions influenced by agriculture, commercial activity, migration and maritime trade.

Surti specialityIdentifying feature
UndhiyuMixed winter vegetables and muthia
PonkTender green sorghum grains
LochoSoft, steamed gram-based preparation
Surti ghariRich sweet containing milk solids and ghee

Tribal food traditions

The forested and hilly eastern belt of Gujarat has distinct agricultural and tribal food traditions. In the Dang district, the District Census Handbook of Census 2011 records nagli, maize, jowar and rice among the principal grains traditionally consumed by local communities.

These traditions demonstrate the importance of combining regional agriculture with other locally available resources. Fish and meat also form part of the food customs of several tribal communities.

Seasonal and festival foods

The availability of crops and other ingredients changes during the year. Gujarat's culinary calendar reflects these seasonal changes as well as religious and social occasions.

Season or occasionAssociated foodFeature
Winter and UttarayanUndhiyuSeasonal vegetables and muthia
Winter in SuratPonkTender sorghum
SummerAamrasMango pulp
DussehraFafda and jalebiSavoury and sweet combination
DiwaliCholafali and ghughraFestive snacks and sweets

Undhiyu and its traditional preparation

Undhiyu commonly includes winter vegetables such as beans, brinjal, potatoes, purple yam and plantain, together with seasoned vegetable dumplings called muthia.

Its name is associated with the Gujarati word for upside down. In a traditional preparation, ingredients are cooked in an inverted earthen pot. Modern undhiyu is also prepared in ordinary cooking vessels.

Food and community identity

Gujarati food culture includes the vegetarian traditions of Jain and Vaishnava communities, coastal fish-based diets, tribal food systems, Muslim culinary traditions and Parsi cuisine.

Parsi dhansak, for example, combines pulses and vegetables with meat in its traditional non-vegetarian form. Such examples demonstrate that the cuisine of Gujarat cannot be reduced to a single regional or religious food pattern.

Prelims focus

  • Ringan no olo and bajri no rotlo are characteristic Kathiawadi preparations.
  • Dabeli is associated with Kutch.
  • Ponk consists of tender sorghum grains, not pearl millet.
  • Undhiyu, locho and ghari are important Surti specialities.
  • Nagli, maize, jowar and rice are traditional grains of the Dang region.
  • Undhiyu is associated with winter, while aamras is associated with summer.

[References: Gujarat Tourism, Gujarati Cuisines, Rotlo, Dabeli, Undhiyu and Festival and Seasonal Fare sections; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Gujarati-Food; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Food Trail: Eat Your Way Through Surat's Gastronomic Delights and West regional cuisine profile; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: The Dangs, Part A, Analytical Note, Major Characteristics of the District. The Dang food description is historical documentation associated with Census 2011, not a current dietary survey. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
